children: The odds of the U.S. passing an AI safety bill before 2027 have fallen sharply on Polymarket, even as warnings about the risks of advanced artificial intelligence have intensified in Washington and Silicon Valley.

Polymarket data showed the probability at 17% on Sept. 15, down from a spike to about 45% on Sept. 10. The one-week chart showed the sharp jump came after reports that a bipartisan group of senators was working on legislation aimed at imposing safety requirements on developers of advanced AI models.
A bipartisan AI safety bill from senators Amy Klobuchar, Ted Cruz, and John Thune may be introduced as early as next week,

The proposed legislation is still being negotiated and would seek to make AI companies responsible for addressing potentially catastrophic risks from their systems. Among the ideas discussed is a legal “duty of care” for developers, requiring them to design AI systems with safeguards against major risks, Reuters reported.

The push for legislation has gained urgency following a series of warnings from AI researchers and industry executives. OpenAI (OPEAI) has advocated mandatory national safety requirements based on the capabilities of advanced models, including outside testing, cybersecurity protections, and incident reporting. CEO Sam Altman endorsed the idea and said his company would also grant independent evaluators employee-like access.
The debate has also been fueled by increasingly stark warnings about whether advanced AI could ultimately threaten human survival. Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic
researcher, resigned this month and warned that people building advanced AI believe it could potentially kill humans by the end of the decade.

Anthropic alignment researcher Evan Hubinger separately put the probability of AI causing human extinction within the next decade at more than 10%, a personal estimate rather than a scientific consensus.
) CEO Dario Amodei called for deliberately slowing improvements in the most powerful AI systems so that safety research and oversight can catch up.

Amodei has also called for the industry to slow the pace of AI development, warning that AI agents could potentially gain the ability to control large parts of the internet within six to 12 months if safeguards fail to keep up. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk have backed the need for greater caution.

The warnings have put pressure on lawmakers to act, but the political path remains uncertain. Senate Majority Leader John Thune has backed congressional involvement and is working with Democrats and Republicans on possible legislation.

House Speaker Mike Johnson said Congress should consult the leaders of the nation’s largest artificial intelligence companies before moving ahead with broad federal regulations, arguing that lawmakers cannot afford to rush legislation governing the rapidly advancing technology.

With Congress facing a crowded schedule ahead of the November midterm elections, the prediction market is now pricing in less than a one-in-five chance that an AI safety bill will become law before 2027.

title: The AI safety bill rally is already unraveling
